title: Inside our 6-stage screening process
excerpt: How we narrow hundreds of CVs down to a shortlist you'll actually want to interview.
body: Every hiring manager knows the pain of a bloated shortlist: twenty profiles, three phone screens, and nobody who quite fits. Our six-stage process exists so that the profiles you see have already been measured against the role, not just matched on keywords.

1. Need analysis. Before we source anyone, we spend 20 to 30 minutes with the hiring manager. We ask what the person will actually do in their first six months, what the team is missing today, which skills are must-haves and which can be learned, and why the last person in the role succeeded or left. This brief is what every later stage is measured against.

2. Sourcing. We search our own talent pool of past applicants first, then reach out through referrals and targeted outreach to people who are not actively looking. Our matching tools rank candidates by skills, but a recruiter reads every profile before we call anyone.

3. Candidate evaluation. Each candidate has a structured screening call that covers the role's core skills, notice period, salary expectations and reasons for moving. For technical and finance roles we add a short skills assessment. Only candidates who clear this call move forward.

4. Interview presentation. You receive a short, curated shortlist, usually three to five people, with a recruiter note on every profile explaining why they fit, any gaps we found and what they expect. You can respond to each profile with Interested, Maybe or Not a fit, and we adjust the search as we learn from your feedback.

5. Background checks. Before an offer, we verify employment history, education and references, with the candidate's consent. It is far cheaper to find a discrepancy now than three months after joining.

6. Offer and closure. We manage salary negotiation, the resignation and notice period, and stay in touch with the candidate until joining day. Most drop-offs happen between offer and joining, so this is where a recruiter's follow-up matters most.
The result is fewer interviews, faster decisions and better retention. If you would like to see how this works for a role you are hiring for, share your requirement on our Hire a Team page.

title: 7 resume fixes that get more interview calls
excerpt: Small, practical changes our recruiters wish every candidate made.
body: Our recruiters read hundreds of resumes every week, and most of them are spending only a few seconds on each one before deciding to read on. These seven fixes are the ones we most often wish candidates had made.

1. Lead with impact, not duties. "Responsible for month-end closing" tells us your job title. "Cut month-end close from 8 days to 5 by automating bank reconciliations" tells us why we should call you. Add a number wherever you honestly can: revenue, time saved, team size, tickets resolved.

2. Tailor the top third to the role. The summary and first few bullet points are what gets read. Rewrite them for each application so they reflect the job description, including the exact skills it lists, as long as you genuinely have them.

3. Put your key skills where they can be found. Add a short skills line near the top with the tools and technologies you use day to day. Recruiters and matching software both search for these, and a skill buried in paragraph six is easy to miss.

4. Keep it short and clean. One page for up to five years of experience, two pages at most for senior roles. Use a simple layout with standard headings, no tables or text inside images, and save it as a PDF so it looks the same on every screen.

5. Make your basics easy to find. Your phone number, email, current city and notice period should be at the top. Notice period matters more than many candidates realise, and leaving it out often means a call that only exists to ask for it.

6. Explain gaps and short stints briefly. A one-line note such as "Career break for family care" or "Contract role, project completed" answers the question before it is asked. Unexplained gaps tend to be read in the least generous way.

7. Proofread, then ask someone else to. Check names of tools, companies and your own contact details. A single typo in your email address means we can't reach you at all, and errors in a resume suggest the same carelessness in the job.

title: Contract vs permanent staffing: which fits your team?
excerpt: A quick guide to choosing the right hiring model for projects, peaks and long-term growth.
body: Choosing between contract and permanent hiring is not only a budget decision. It affects how fast you can start, how much risk you carry and what kind of capability you are building. Here is how we help clients think it through.

Contract staffing gives you speed and flexibility. The professional is on our payroll for a fixed term while working on your projects, and we handle salary, statutory compliance such as PF and ESI, and benefits. You receive one monthly invoice. It suits defined projects, seasonal peaks, cover for leave, and roles you are still validating.

Permanent hiring builds long-term capability and culture. The person joins your payroll from day one, and you pay a one-time success fee only when they join, usually backed by a replacement guarantee. It is the right choice for core roles, leadership positions and anyone who will hold critical knowledge about your business.

Contract-to-hire sits between the two. The person starts as a contractor and converts to your payroll after an agreed period. Both sides can evaluate fit in real work before committing, which is especially useful for new teams or roles that are hard to assess in interviews.

A few questions usually make the choice clear. Will this work still exist in 12 months? How quickly do you need someone productive? Do you have the HR capacity to onboard and manage compliance yourself? And how costly would a wrong hire be in this role?

Many of our clients use a mix: a permanent core team supported by contract specialists for peaks and projects. Talk to us about your roadmap and we will recommend a combination that balances cost, speed and continuity.
